title: Prostate cancer screening using short MRI and advanced blood tests in younger, high-risk men
official: Imperial Prostate 15 - Risk Adapted Detection using Abbreviated magnetic Resonance imaging
summary:
Background and study aims
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in men in the UK: over 60,000 men are diagnosed annually and more than 12,000 die from the disease. It is one of the only major cancers without a national screening programme. This is because the traditional test to diagnose prostate cancer, a blood test called prostate specific antigen (PSA), can be "positive" for reasons other than cancer (known as a false positive), leading to unnecessary tests in up to two thirds of men, but also missing important cancers (false negative). Newer tests, such as MRI scans and advanced blood tests that incorporate genetic markers, could improve how prostate cancer is detected, especially in men at higher risk, but are yet to be formally assessed. This study aims to explore whether a combination of modern tests could be used to screen younger men (aged 40-49) who are at increased risk of prostate cancer due to factors such as family history, being of Black ethnicity, or having certain genetic mutations. 

Who can participate?
Men aged between 40 and 49 who have one or more of the following risk factors for prostate cancer:
1.	Be of Black or mixed Black ethnicity
2.	Have a first-degree family member with prostate, breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer
3.	Have a genetic mutation called BRCA1 or BRCA2.

Men who have had recent prostate cancer investigations or screening tests cannot take part.

What does the study involve?
Participants will attend a single visit where they will have:
1.	A short, non-invasive MRI scan of the prostate (lasting 10-15 minutes)
2.	A standard blood test for PSA
3.	A blood test for the genetic biomarker Stockholm3
4.	An optional finger-prick blood test (capillary sample)

If any test suggests a higher risk of cancer, participants will be offered a prostate biopsy as part of routine NHS care. The study will assess how well these tests work alone and together, how acceptable they are to patients, and whether this approach could form the basis of a future targeted screening programme. It will also evaluate potential harms, such as unnecessary biopsies, and patient experience. The results will help determine whether earlier, more targeted screening could improve prostate cancer detection whilst reducing harms in men at highest risk.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
It is not known if taking part will result in direct, guaranteed benefits for individual participants, as the interventions being tested are experimental and their effectiveness is not yet fully established. Nevertheless, it is likely that some participants may experience personal health benefits. For example, earlier detection of potentially significant prostate cancer could lead to more timely treatment options and potentially reduce the risk of prostate cancer-related mortality.

Each element of the Prostate Health Check is low-risk, and the tests are non-invasive. Some men may feel claustrophobic in the Prostagram MRI, and the blood tests can be uncomfortable but shouldn’t be painful. As with all medical tests, there is a risk of false-positive and false-negative results, as none of the tests are expected to be 100% accurate. A false positive test could mean that a man is offered further investigations that do not lead to a diagnosis of prostate cancer and therefore could be considered unnecessary. A false negative test means that prostate cancer is missed, though the risk of this is low. Sometimes, the tests lead to a diagnosis of a “low risk” prostate cancer that wouldn’t have been diagnosed if the participant had not undergone the Prostate Health Checks. These low risk cancers do not need treatment but require long term monitoring.

Where is the study run from?
The study is sponsored by Imperial College London, and the Prostate Health Checks will take place at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2026 to October 2028. 

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health & Care Research (NIHR), UK.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Nikhil Mayor, imperial.radar@nhs.net and radar.study@imperial.ac.uk.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Male
2. Aged 45-49 years with family history of first-degree relative diagnosed with prostate, breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer (any ethnicity but Black) or
3. Aged 40-44 years with family history of first-degree relative diagnosed with prostate, breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer (any ethnicity) or
4. Aged 40-44 years and of Black ethnicity or
5. Aged 40-49 years and known BRCA1/2 mutation
6. Capacity to provide informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
1. Known history of prostate cancer
2. PSA test, other prostate biomarker in the preceding two years
3. Any history of prostate MRI or prostate biopsy
4. Urinary tract infection or prostatitis in the preceding three months
5. Estimated life expectancy less than 10 years
